utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Robovic. Will you please first give your full name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Zulfo Robovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, you were born in Trebinje in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1958, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: From 1986, however, you've been living in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was -- I must apologise. There's a misprint, both in English and B/C/S version. Mr. Robovic doesn't live in Capljina since 1986, but since 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You're married and your wife is a physician and you have one child?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are of Muslim ethnicity and of Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were never a member of the Communist Party of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, when the Party of Democratic Action was founded in 1990, you became a member of that party; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And from October 1992 you were a member of the executive committee of the Party for Democratic Action in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, later, in February 1993, you joined the new Muslim party, Muslim Democratic Party; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, you graduated from the electrical engineering faculty in Sarajevo in 1982?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You began your career by working for Electroprivreda, which is an electric utility company generating and distributing electric energy?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you worked as an engineer, and subsequently you became the head of the data processing department in Mostar. Will you tell the Court what you do now? What is your current job?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now work for the Croatian Chamber of Commerce and I'm head of its office in Mostar, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the population census of 1991, in the town of Mostar there was about an equal number of Croats and Muslims; that is, Muslims accounted for some 34.3 per cent, and Croats accounted for one per cent less, that is, 33.3; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And there were also about 17 per cent of Serbs and other peoples?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After the first multi-party elections, which took place in 1990, the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina won some 40 per cent of votes. I'm referring to the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Around 40 seats, and yes, about 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In your summary, in paragraph 7, you tell us that almost a hundred per cent of the Croats voted for the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas Serbs, by and large, voted for their chief party, the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, the SDA, the Party for Democratic Action, fared very bad in the elections because only about 20 per cent of you, the Muslims, voted for that party?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So that of some 100 elected councilmen to the Mostar hall, the HDZ had some 40, 45 councilmen, the Party for Democratic Action only 19, and the Serb Democratic Party only 17.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps there is no need to speak about the reasons for the defeat of the Party for Democratic Action in those elections. But in your summary you say that this was largely contributed to by the leftist orientation of the Muslims in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And that is why they voted for other parties?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. They voted for leftist parties, the party for -- the reform section and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In 1991, and the Court has already heard about it, in September 1991, the JNA deployed the reserve force in the area of Mostar, and that was the time when the members of the SDA -- of the SDS withdrew from the government and the municipal government in Mostar, so that the Party for Democratic action and the HDZ organised life and the defence of Mostar by themselves.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A large percentage of Muslims, some 70 or 80 per cent of you Muslims, did not realise the danger yet, or rather had a rather passive attitude to the threat --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I prefer matters not to be led, really, on these topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ask in a non-leading fashion, please. What happened next? Perhaps the witness can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So Mr. Robovic, what was the attitude of the majority of Muslims to the threat which became evident after the Serb forces were deployed around Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were in the -- we had a lot of problems with the Muslims in Mostar because they did not see those people as reservists who had come to occupy them. They behaved very casually, and I must say that because of this, shall I say, the Yugoslav option of those Muslims at the time, they simply did not think that things would happen as they did happen later on. We tried to inform those people, we tried to defend those people. We had the information in view of what had been happening in Croatia, in Vukovar, and Dubrovnik, in East Slavonia that it was bound to happen too, that they would attack Mostar because they had taken the -- all the predominant hill features and they had a very good view of the whole city of Mostar and according to the knowledge that we had, they simply could not only besiege but suffocate Sarajevo just as they did with -- suffocate Mostar just as they did with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was waiting for the interpretation to end, but I must ask you, Mr. Robovic to slow down a little bit because we have to help the interpreters. You mentioned the Serb aggression or rather the JNA aggression against Croatia, did the Party for Democratic Action and the HDZ, generally speaking, and in Mostar, in particular, cooperate basically? Did they share the attitude to that?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Always, absolutely. At that time the HDZ and the SDA shared, had identical views at that time and the -- both at the level of the regional boards and the city of Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are aware, aren't you, that a certain number of Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily from Herzegovina, but also a certain number of Muslims went to the Republic of Croatia to fight against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: True. We Muslims in Mostar and this time showed in Sarajevo too, we had it very bad when Vukovar and then Dubrovnik was attacked, and it finally stirred even those who were very passive towards this Yugoslav armada, that is, the Yugoslav forces. We all had a uniform view regarding the need to defend ourselves so that we and the Croats together went to defend Dubrovnik or the areas around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, towards the end of 1991 when the number of incidents with the Serbs increased, did the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, at the local level in Mostar, as far as you know, armed you, the Muslims, too or not?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Mostar Croats armed Muslims as well so that they could defend themselves against the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At about the same time the Patriotic League was established; whose army was that, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: The Party for Democratic Action at the republican level, at the Bosnia-Herzegovina level; that is, in some of the towns where the Party for Democratic Action was active, and that was in the majority of towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Mostar as well, through its activists, organised the Patriotic League as a force which would prevent those Serb attacks and provocations or rather save the bare lives of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this was an army which was organised by the Party for Democratic Action and you were an active member of it at that time.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Since we are on the subject of the SDA, would you know or, that is, you must know that the SDA, as a party, was also formed in the rest of Yugoslavia, that is, today, Yugoslavia, that is, in the Republic of Croatia and in the broader area?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite correct. The SDA was also founded and active in Sandzak, that is Serbia, that is Yugoslavia, and there was also a sister party in the Republic of Croatia and it was at that time headed and I believe it still is by Professor Semso Tankovic. And in Sandzak, in Serbia, the party and there was also established the National Council of the Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And who was the supreme commander of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I think the supreme commander, that is, the man who was above on the top of all these things was Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And tell us, please, who were the founders of the Patriotic League in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: In Mostar, pursuant to the instructions of the centre of the staff, the Patriotic League was founded by brothers Hadziosmanovic. They were among the founding members of the SDA in Mostar and the region and they conducted all the activities relative to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: These forces of the Patriotic League in Mostar subsequently grew into an independent Mostar battalion or whatever it was called?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was simply how it happened so that it was the conclusion of the party, the autonomous or independent battalion was formed because there was some problems, whether it was a TO from the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the question was whether it could be the protagonist and the guarantor of the defence of these areas so that the Patriotic League or whatever grew into an independent Mostar battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And tell us, this independent Mostar battalion, was it, for a while part, of the Croat Defense Council?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. It was part of the Croat Defense Council, that is, the staff of the Croat Defense Council was superior to these independent battalion in Mostar, that is, only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. We can then move on Your Honours, moving to paragraph 11. Mr. Robovic, will you tell us, please, in late 1991 and early 1992 because of the Serb operations in East Herzegovina, the Serbs expelled a large number of refugees from those areas. Where did those people go?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I think of those times, I think nobody can remain indifferent to that, it was a general expression of everything that was called Muslim because in that part of east Herzegovina there was very few Croats and those -- it was a general stampede, if I can use that word, when talking to people. And people sought shelter in various areas because in Mostar, there were Croats and Muslims living and they were coming there looking to protect their lives so we organised accommodation for those people and we simply shared with them all we had. We welcomed them, we both -- both we the local Muslims and the Croats welcomed them; that is, they were not accommodated in Mostar alone, they were also accommodated in Medjurgorje, Citluk, Ljubuski, Capljina, that is, all over the area. And naturally in Croatia too because it was organised with the assistance of international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, how many thousands of refugees did you accommodate on the west bank -- on the west side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we never really kept any regular books, but according to our knowledge and when we distributed food to those hapless people, I think there was perhaps as many as 20.000 of our, that is, my countrymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you said that the majority of those refugees were Muslims, because they constituted the predominant population in east Herzegovina on the east side?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, true. These are the municipalities of Trebinje, Gacko, Bileca and Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you used plural, you said "We organised an accommodation," "We helped," and so on and so forth. Do you mean Muslims only or Croats too?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims. Because we did it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when accommodating refugees, did you try to also provide them with some religious facilities so they could practice their faith?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: That was one of the -- yes, demands, and that the Crisis Staff at that time and subsequently the municipal HVO government organised their accommodation in the student hostel and the mufti centre was also there, established there, with the residents of Efendiz, that is Mostar mufti, and they were in the -- we made a make-shift mosque. And at that time, I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, I'm going to interrupt you. We've had a huge amount of detail in this case, and unless this is a particularly relevant point, we needn't go into it. Let's move on. Mr. Naumovski, paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, at that time you became a member of the executive board of the SDA in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Was it 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Oh, 1992. Sorry. But even before that, as a party activist, and particularly after the date when you informally became a member of the executive board, you attended numerous meetings with representatives of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Mostar, that is; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. But let me explain. We reconstructed the executive board of the SDA because the President Hadziosmanovic wanted us to include in the executive board as many professionals, Muslims -- and we can see that there were a number of university teachers, physicians, successful managers, and also I joined it as an engineer -- because we intended to modernise the party and open it, because during the previous period of time it had a rather large rural representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your contacts with the HDZ at the time were practically -- had to do only with the defence and organisation of civilian life, not only in the city of Mostar but also in the municipality of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Before you became a member of the party's executive board, in April 1992, that is, 29th of April, 1992, the SDA and the HDZ agreed on some fundamentals regarding their work, and that is the defence?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is one of, I should say, key decisions for the whole area of Mostar and its environs taken on the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And what was the gist of this agreement? Whose duty was it to defend Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: According to that agreement, the Crisis Staff, which derived from the Municipal Assembly of Mostar, which could not function, turned over, or rather agreed, or rather decided to charge the Croat Defence Council with the defence of Mostar, and the Mostar Battalion, and the -- the Independent Battalion, consisting mostly of Muslims. So that the Croat Defence Council, its Crisis Staff in Mostar, was entrusted with the defence of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind Your Honours. It is -- the document relative to this is D271/1 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But regardless of this Independent Battalion which was -- which consisted mostly of Muslims, there were also Muslims in those 13 Croat battalions which were directly subordinated to the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: It is. That is, as far as we're aware, and according to our records, Muslims accounted for some 27 to 30 per cent in those battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mean those, if I may call them so, mixed battalions?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Battalions of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps just one detail. This Independent Battalion, which consisted of Muslims only, it then grew into the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it did.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: And after a decision of President Izetbegovic at the time and amendments to the decisions on defence, after that it was transformed and became the 4th Corps. It became a part of that corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript it says -- when I spoke about this document, I said it was D277/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. We can move on. So after 29th of April, 1992, that is, after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me get this straight. What is the document? The original in the transcript is 271/1. You later simply refer to 277/1. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an error in the transcript. It is not 271, but 277. And this is the agreement between the SDA and HDZ -- that is, the Crisis Staff -- that the HVO should take over the -- should assume the responsibility for the defence of the city of Mostar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, following the agreement of April 1992, the SDA and HDZ formed an agreement to establish a new municipal government with equal numbers from both parties.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian HVO government was established. The president was Jadran Topic, and I believe there were ten departments, and the staff was 50/50. Hamdija Jahic, Zlatko Udovicic, Maslo Kazazic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My apologies. Perhaps we should not go into such detail. But the representations was about 50/50 between Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After fierce fighting in June of 1992, the JNA and the Bosnian Serb army were defeated at Mostar and the eastern bank of the Neretva River, and these parts were liberated but completely destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. About 90 per cent was devastated, both family homes and different business facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After, could a number of refugees move back to eastern Herzegovina, those who took refuge in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They went back to try to clear up the rubble, but there were no communications. The infrastructure was completely destroyed. And so only a few people went back to clear up and perhaps prepare to rebuild.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can move on to paragraph 15. In August 1992 a political dispute arose between the Muslims and the Croats concerning political symbols in use. But the causes, the underlying causes, must have been others too.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: At that time there was a certain division within the regional and the local SDA. Orucevic tried to unseat Hadziosmanovic as the president of the party. And then of course the reasons were sought for political measures to dismiss Hadziosmanovic and his followers. So in one executive board meeting -- this was a wider meeting -- there was talk about withdrawing Muslims from the local government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this was the position of the party, or part of the party, that the Muslims who were within the government should pull out?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those Muslims who made part of the HVO government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did Muslims follow these instructions of the party?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: We had some raised voices in one of the meetings of the party. I personally believe that it was not right for us to pull out, and two or three members agreed with me. Some reserved their judgement. So that only Mr. Udovicic and Nijaz Berhamovic stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After your representatives followed the instruction of the party and pulled out, who stayed in the government? Only Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Only Croats. And as I said, also Mr. Udovicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps another detail. How did these frictions within the party end up? What was the result, both at the regional and city level?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: We were seeking a compromise. At that time the reorganisation of the executive board was followed by the first visit of President Izetbegovic to Mostar. This was in the period between 15th and 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1992. We asked for his opinion concerning this dispute, and a compromise was reached that Mr. Hadziosmanovic remain the president of the municipal party and that Zijad Demirovic succeed him in the regional board of the SDA, which included Konjic, Jablanica, Capljina municipalities as well, so that was the regional board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what factors started dominating the local politics in Mostar? What forces were these?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: These were the forces that were not for cooperation with Croats. There was a military top, headed by Arif Pasalic; a number of imams, that is, religion leaders; and a number of intellectuals who were organised in a Herzegovinian Muslim group, looking to bypass the SDA led by Hadziosmanovic, and also with Demirovic, who took over the regional SDA board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: How did they manage to bypass the SDA headquarters? Did they form another body?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they established another body. We always questioned its legality, because it was never properly registered. It was called the Herzegovinian Muslim Council. They issued press releases, they held press conferences, and that was the way they conducted their activity and strained relationships within the city and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did this Herzegovinian Muslim Council manage to take over the authority, the power in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Hadziosmanovic, Cemalovic, myself, and some others who were in the executive board started losing influence under the pressure of the Herzegovinian Muslim Council, including the military top and the imams. They also wanted to take control over some of our humanitarian activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We will come to that a bit later. But by taking over all the activities, did this council establish some kind of parallel power? On the one hand there was the HVO, which was legal through the agreements with the SDA, and now there was a new council being established. So was there parallel power at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: They tried to take over and control all the Muslim activities in that region and that period. So they were active, but their legality has never been clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You have mentioned that this Independent Mostar Battalion separated itself out of the HVO and it became the nucleus of the 4th ABiH Corps headed by Arif Pasalic. Where was it headquartered?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: The corps was headquartered in the Vranica company premises. This is in the western part of Mostar, when I look at it from today's perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Paragraph 17. You mentioned the Muslim humanitarian organisation, the Red Crescent. Who headed this organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: It was Arif Hadziosmanovic, one of the Hadziosmanovic brothers. I was also fairly active in it. It was created precisely because of what had happened before the sudden influx of Muslims from eastern Herzegovina, and there was a need for a humanitarian organisation in Mostar. We had -- we were assigned -- we were given offices and warehouses from the HVO government, and the organisation was properly registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Along with the Caritas, which is an arm of the Catholic church and other humanitarian organisations, both of these organisations helped all citizens regardless of their faith?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Caritas even helped us out so that we can distribute some food and clothing to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the new leadership of the Red Crescent humanitarian organisation continued to care for all citizens regardless of their faith?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: They were organised in some other areas as well, but they endeavored and they succeeded to simply force this organisation out of operation. I don't know where they were moved after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mentioned the Hadziosmanovic family, maybe you can tell us more. Are they a very prominent family?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... any more evidence on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness spoke about the stratification of the SDA and who was influential at the time. The Hadziosmanovic family, was a very prominent family in Mostar, it's an old Mostar family, and they had quite a lot of influence at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I cannot think it's going to assist us. Why don't you move on to paragraph 18 dealing with it in a neutral way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was exactly my idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Robovic, who formed the Elektroprivredra power utility company?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: The SDA executive board reached a meeting that a group of us negotiated with the HDZ in order to organise the power supply and also to the staffing of the utility company; so in other words, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So in other words, it was an agreement. For the Trial Chamber to gain a better picture, what area was this utility company supposed to cover?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: This was to be a wider area. This would have covered a much wider area than the current western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps -- how much Croats and how many Muslims lived in this area where -- that was served by the Elektroprivredra?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the 1990 census, the figures that we had at the time -- there was 60 per cent of Croats versus 35 to 38 per cent of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And how many people were supposed to be in the executive board of the Elektroprivredra?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: We reached the agreement that the executive board would consist of five members, two Muslims and three Croats, but the president was to have been a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. And the Croat would have been --

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Executive manager and in the top management which would include six persons, there would have been four Croats and two Muslims, but the production manager covering six power plants between Rama and Capljina was to be an ethnic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In regard of the frictions within the SDA leadership, did that reflect on those Muslims who worked in this Elektroprivredra of HZ HB? Were you asked something?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: The group around Demirovic and Orucevic assisted by Pasalic expressly demanded that we step down and leave the Elektroprivredra, and they did it in a fairly rude way also.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Elektroprivredra, sometime around June 1992, employed about 800 people in total. Were these people paid? Were these people discriminated in terms of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No, the Elektroprivredra took over all the employees except for the Serbian ones who had left so that all employees who lived and worked between Rama and Capljina continued to come to work and continued to be provided salaries based on the payrolls that existed and their everything has been properly accounted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. We can move on to paragraph 19. In the late fall of 1992, the SDA held a large congress in Zenica, can you in brief, but really very briefly, sum up what kind of a party the SDA became after this congress?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: We prepared our delegates in Mostar, they went as -- they -- people who went were Demirovic, Cemalovic, Hadziosmanovic, Salahovic so that we could see where we were going. What was in dispute was whether for us in Mostar -- many people asked questions including myself, how -- what was our relationship to the HZ HB and that was also the question that they raised in Zenica. I believe that the meeting was held on the 11th of November. What was experienced was very unpleasant because they were subject to an orchestrated attack by the SDA of Central Bosnia. They were accused of being another SDA, that they could not have this position towards the Croats. Our members wanted cooperation with the Croats. They were not outvoted; they were simply defeated in this meeting by people like Topcagic from Vakuf and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is not so important.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I think they came with very negative views on what the SDA leadership was telling them. After that, the SDA leadership opted for a more radical approach against Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, was one of the conclusions that you should not participate in the governing bodies of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: As the main board, and I believe at that time, the general secretary was Ceman, they always waived certain papers but I never saw the contents of these documents. They said that they could not take part of the certain government of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, you were obviously not very content with the situation in the party and in February 1993, you left the SDA and you founded a new party?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was following the congress that I mentioned. Perhaps another month we went, somewhat afraid of our own safety, and then we had to separate ourselves out and we had to pursue our own views and try to establish a permanent cooperation between the Muslims and Croats. This is why we decided to form a new party, the Muslim Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, Their Honours have had ample opportunities to hear about the conflict which broke out around 9 May. You were not there at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was travelling on business for Elektroprivredra.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know precisely who attacked whom and what happened during the two days when you were not there?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: There were different stories. My own view of things as the pieces of the puzzle started falling into place was that on that morning, the units of the 4th Corps attacked the units in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This is the conclusion you drew from your contacts with people, but regardless of -- but with respect of the different sides, people had different views?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I formed my conclusions based on certain insights which I gained subsequently, but some of the pieces fell into place a year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you, at some point later, learn that there had been an order of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't lead on these matters. Clearly they're controversial. We don't want to hear your evidence, Mr. Naumovski, we want to hear the witness'.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with due respect, I just wanted to ask him whether he had heard about it. I did not mean to lead him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know any details about this order or not?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I saw some details a long time -- actually a long time after, but also some things that were going on in the city, that is, displaying of some army symbols in the city. All -- I think that the army attempted to move into the areas which was to be a demarcation point between the two military organisations and Pasalic was behind that. The orders were issued to the 4th Army Corps to move deeper into Mostar into the zone of the HVO and the signs were put up in -- on buildings where the army was supposed to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said that Arif Pasalic was the commander of the 4th Army Corps but then there was Mr. Zelenika, who was he?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenika was the commander of the HVO forces in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In these chaotic times in May and June 1993, did your party negotiate with the HVO government in Mostar how to overcome the tensions, how to alleviate the tensions?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: We were seeking for ways to do so. We contacted a number of people in Herceg-Bosna to use political means to calm down the tensions and to -- so that we can provide humanitarian aid and we can restore some kind of normalcy. Whether we were successful or not is another question. But there was an intense effort at all levels in Herceg-Bosna to try and calm down and stabilize the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, the witness said earlier that signs were put up on buildings where the army was supposed to move. I'd like to ask him whether he actually saw any of these signs or is this based on what he was told.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Robovic, after the outbreak of conflict, the majority of Muslims who lived on the western side of Mostar along with the refugees moved to the eastern side?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, did a significant number of Muslims stay on in the western part?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Again, we fought for every single man as the party because it was a wartime. So we put in a lot of effort and managed to keep about 8.000 Muslims in the so-called western side which is under the HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: These are people who used to work there before in the hospital and all other places, they continued to work there?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they continued to work there at Elektroprivredra, at the university, hospital, schools, because those were the only things still working, the economy had collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When we discuss your activities in that period, did you at any time see any document or did you ever hear in your contacts that you had with the HDZ at the time that there was an official policy of discrimination towards all non-Croats in the Mostar region. Did you ever hear anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw any document in that regard nor did I ever hear about any orders or decisions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on to the next paragraph, 25 onward and that is your service in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Mr. Robovic, in October of 1993, you were appointed Minister of Reconstruction Development of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were not a member of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, at that time, you were still the member of this party which you had formed in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were a member of the Muslim Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and a member of its Presidency and they continued to work when I was appointed -- even when I was appointed the Minister of Reconstruction and Development and its president was Armin Pohara, I mean of the Muslim democratic party of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who appointed you? Who was it that appointed you?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: To that office, it was proposed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and I was appointed by the president of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Master of Sciences, Mate Boban. It was confirmed by the house of representatives in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, could you please tell us, if you remember, how many ministries were there in the government of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: There are documents about this and I can't really remember, but I believe there were 15 of them, two or three departments, a few services and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As a government minister in the HR HB government and your party duties, did you then try to help to prevent Muslim/Croat conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: My guiding principle throughout the time was participate, negotiate, pursue agreement and optimal solutions in a situation for the solution of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a community of three peoples; that is, I continued through my activities to seek ways and means to the solution of that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Court has already heard a great deal about the effects indicated in paragraph 26 so perhaps there is no need to go back to this paragraph, and if there are any questions you will have an opportunity to answer them later. In your ministry which you worked, how many, what was its staff?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Its staff was about 18. We paid all the dues, all the taxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And how many of those 18 were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: There were three [as interpreted] Muslims. One was a professional associate, two typists and one person working for the automatic data processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, as a minister in the government of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, you must have also had an idea, had a broader idea about the employment of Muslims in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and I believe you are the right man to answer my question. Were Muslims represented elsewhere too? Did they work for other departments in the judiciary health care and so on so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were Muslims at the university. They were members of the steering board of the university, in the clinics, school principals, secondary and elementary schools, physicians. They were also in ministries. But this means that the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna where it wielded authority had no discriminatory positions regarding the question not only of employing Muslims, but also other people under its authority – non-Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the 9 witness could be shown document 276/1, tab 5. 276/1, tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you please look at this document, Mr. Robovic. It is a list of persons of Muslim ethnicity who worked in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, Croat Republic, tab 5.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you please just cast a look at the list. Do you know most of these people personally? And is it true that they worked full time for institutions of the Herceg Community of Herceg-Bosna, and then you will also see a list for the Herceg -- for the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know quite a number of people from the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You know them personally?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I know them -- yes, I know their names, and personally, yes, the majority of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And they work for those institutions, as it says here?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So as not to waste any more time, we can move on. Mr. Robovic, your party, the Muslim Democratic Party, maintained direct contacts with the leadership of the Croat Republic, the presidency of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, that is, the president of the HVO, that is, your immediate superior, Dr. Jadranka Prlic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, insofar as operative matters were concerned, it was the executive power, that is, Mr. Prlic. And as for political attitudes and how we saw individual options, that was exclusively with the president, Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your party founded a humanitarian organisation called Esperanza. Who helped you to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: We asked, and I confirmed. There were 8.000 Muslims in Mostar alone, and the war was going on and most of them could not find any jobs, because, you know, I mean, those who worked worried, because even Croats were left jobless. But then we had to find a solution to provide those people with some basic necessities, basic foodstuffs. And we found an area where the government of Herceg-Bosna and the government of Mostar helped us to put that area into order, to make a warehouse, offices, and so on and so forth, and reported to the record, all through the humanitarian organisation Esperanza, which was founded by the Muslim Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Until when was your party active?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Our party was active until the conclusion of the Washington Accords, when we sat down and I suggested to President Pohara to stop the activities, because that agreement had put an end to the imposed conflict between Croats and Muslims, and we left it to the then-signatories to embark on the implementation of these agreements. We did not want to politically interfere, so as not to make the situation more difficult, because we had achieved what we had been pursuing from the beginning, and that was that the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the victims of the greater Serb aggression, set up the joint government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you left it to the two basic political parties to discuss all the future issues for that country, that is, the two principal political parties of the Muslims and the Croats: HDZ and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. We didn't agree with the HDZ policy, but, as I've already said, we froze our activities. The party did not close down; we simply froze our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can move on to paragraph 29. Mr. Robovic, you are personally aware that in November 1993 several thousand refugees from Vares arrived in the city of Mostar. And they were, for the most part, Croats, but there were also some Muslims amongst them, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I do not think they came to Mostar, or rather I'm sure they did not. I think they were evacuated to areas around Stolac. There were some Muslims, 150, 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Through your humanitarian organisation, Esperanza, you talked to those people. Why did they leave Vares?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: We sent our party activists to that place where they were received so that, together with the department for the reception of refugees of the government of Herceg-Bosna to accommodate those people and provide them with basic necessities, and they made statements to our activists, to the Esperanza activists, that quite simply they had also been expelled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina because, according to some information of those liberators, well, they had collaborated with Croats in that area, and that was the principal reason for their flight from Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Paragraph 30 of your summary. Perhaps I could ask you it differently. I thought of skipping over it, but perhaps you will answer it, if need be. I believe that the Court has already heard a great deal about it, and if need be, you can answer questions about it in a subsequent examination. Since you worked in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, you had an insight into the personnel who worked there, people who discharged different offices. What was the quality of people who worked with you, for instance, from the HVO who worked with you in various ministries, as for their professionalism, approach to daily problems, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that I take pride in having worked with those people, from President Jadranka Prlic down to various extra services. They were highly capable people, excellent professionals, and they were the basis of the -- they were the basis of building and of reconstruction, of implementation and reconstruction after Washington and Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the institutions of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna were disbanded and they became the institute and so the Federation after these accords. And a large part of their good work that was put in, that is, regulations and so on and so forth, continued then to be enforced in the Federation, and that is the case to this day, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. And international organisations also confirm my view; that is, documents which were adopted in Bosnia-Herzegovina had their permanent value, and they still have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can move on to the next topic, Mr. Robovic, and that is a couple of questions about Mr. Dario Kordic. Could you tell us: When is it that you met Mr. Dario Kordic, and where?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I met Dario Kordic, visually, in late 1993, in Mostar. I think it was the appointment, the confirmation of the House of Representatives of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: By the House of Representatives?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the House of Representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: With Mr. Kordic, you have had plenty of opportunity to talk, and perhaps it would be interesting if you told the Court: You are peers, more or less, but you are of different faiths; you belong to different peoples. Did you ever in your conversations with Mr. Kordic disagree on those fundamental issues concerning joint life and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot but confirm to the Honourable Court that as a government of Herceg-Bosna, we were in Central Bosnia, I think, in spring 1994, and that we talked -- I then personally talked with Mr. Dario Kordic, as the Minister of Reconstruction and Development, about the reconstruction and development of all the areas, regardless of what the future organisation would be, that is, renewal of the supply of power, water, the reconstruction of religious facilities. And we talked of that. We have lived to see the time that, as a Croat, as a Muslim, we could freely voice our opinions in our fatherland, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and regardless of whether anyone was bothered by this, that we could live side by side and we could freely discuss and practice our customs, our traditions, and so on and so forth. I discussed it freely with Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you mentioned your visit to the Lasva Valley, you must have attended quite a number of meetings there. Did you ever hear Mr. Kordic, after the war, that is, at the time when one had to embark upon the reconstruction and repair of all that had been destroyed, did you ever hear him refer badly to not only Muslims, but any other peoples, or was it completely identical to what you were thinking about?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: It went on during the term of office of Mr. Kordic, as the president of the Croat Democratic Union. We then talked, as the president of the party, which -- that is, HDZ, and me, as a minister in the government of Herceg-Bosna. And we were talking about how, through my ministry, we could ensure fundamental life necessities and religious needs of all the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was part of my ministry as the Minister for Reconstruction and Development. And we talked about some major subjects, fundamental topics as I have mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In your summary, included in what paragraph 36 says, and that is the reason why you agreed to testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I still stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You have already answered this question. You said that you met him, that you talked, that you more or less shared views, and those were the basic views which made -- prevailed upon you, and you decided to come to testify.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Because in him I saw energy, I saw the will to implement Washington agreements to the benefit of both peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I think we've made quite a good progress, and we shall be able to complete this before the break. Now we're moving to the last topic. So you spent those hardest years in Mostar, subsequently you became a minister in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. You socialised with people at different levels, both at the city level and at this high level in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and you met quite a number of people.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When I say "very many people," I mean people who were decision-makers, planners, and so on. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Did you ever hear at that high level that any institution in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, ever adopted any policy, any plan, any programme, or anything else, for the elimination or ethnic cleansing of Muslim or other non-Croats from the territories of the Croat Community, that is, Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling this Honourable Court that I neither heard, nor saw, nor gained an impression from conversations that that was the objective, and I would have never agreed, under no conditions whatsoever, to place at the disposal of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna my knowledge and everything else that I could offer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In view of your contacts with the Croats, had there been such a secret plan, if I may call it that, did exist after all, would you have been in a position to learn about it?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I think one could -- yes, one could find that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you ever, when active in the government, hear, from any member of the government, any proposals to that effect, even if informal?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I must say to this Honourable Court: While I was the minister, the government met on about a hundred occasions under very difficult -- in very difficult times -- 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996 -- and there were no discriminatory discussions, let alone decisions, that would be conducive to a discrimination, not only of Muslims, but any other people under the jurisdiction of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, at any of these sessions, and this can be corroborated by documents of the sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let me follow up on what you have just said. Did the institutions in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, aspire to become monoethnic?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: They did not aspire to become monoethnic because the leadership of the community and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna also, that is, during that period when I was in the SDA, asked us to discuss with them the entry of Muslims in the administration of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. At the time of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, there were some agreements, one of them concerned the economy, but also pressure was brought on people who wanted to work, who wanted to participate in the work of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, we are talking about the pressure brought on Muslims, but who by?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, at the time when I was in the SDA, it was by the army structure headed by Pasalic, the Council of the Muslims of Herzegovina, and a part of the SDA headed by Demirovic and Orucevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And perhaps my final question we could conclude with this, as a Muslim, you were a minister of the -- in the government of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna and that is perhaps the best answer to my question as to whether those structures were monoethnic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can make that sort of comment in your speech. Yes, Mr. Naumovski, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Robovic, thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour, just two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Robovic, my name is Mr. Bozidar Kovacic. I am a lawyer and I am the counsel here for the second accused, Mr. Mario Cerkez. I only have two short questions since you are here, so I must take this opportunity even though we didn't meet before. In 1992 and 1993, did you ever have an opportunity to visit Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You've never been there?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is, municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you abreast of the developments, at least, in party channels at least while you were in the SDA about the situation in that part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, we had some discussions and in early 1993, about the situation about the developments in Central Bosnia and its reflections on Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did you, at the time, when you founded the MDSD, Muslim Democratic Party, did you also set up its branch in that part of Bosnia in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Pohara did have some people who were to initiate it, who had reached the stage of setting that up in Central Bosnia but, personally, I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, you said at some point in your testimony not in -- not verbatim, but that was my interpretation, that the SDA had its more extreme forces, and also other forces, that there were different factions in the party; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: There were both factions and had views especially concerning cooperation with Croats and the constitutional organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we briefly say it by saying that the SDA had its radicals and its liberals? I'm talking about the regional board of the SDA board of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But it also held true of the SDA in other parts or particularly that is the area of my concern is Central Bosnia, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned it in my testimony after the main board in Zenica how our members from Herzegovina we had a number of them mostly from Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you I understand you well that the SDA in Central Bosnia were much more radical than your colleagues down there in your region in the region of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: This is my free interpretation on the basis of conversation between our officials in the regional board in Herzegovina, I can confirm that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And just one question more, have you ever met Mr. Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I never met him. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that name during the war in 1992, 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: After the adjournment. Mr. Robovic, we're going to adjourn now until half past 11.00. During the adjournment don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, please. Don't let anybody speak to you about it and that does include members of the Defence team. Yes, we'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Robovic, you have been supplied with a summary of your evidence dated the 18th of June. Who drafted it, please?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: It was, I believe, ten days ago or a week, about ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that first draft, was it in any way altered by lawyers who represent Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this document's been available in the present state and in the present format for the last ten days?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you given any headings or did you just conceive the headings yourself, please?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: This is my statement, what I know, and what I have come up with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I quite understand, but just help me it's a tiny matter of detail, but I just want to know where we've got a document that's broken down into headings and paragraphs, things like personal information and then educational background and so on, the format of the document, was that your idea?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Everything I do in my life is based on my own ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that just to take another tiny example so that we can be quite clear about this, where we see as the last heading on page nine in the English version heading G which says, "No Croat Policy of Persecution". You have it in English as well as in Croatian? Do you see the heading there, "No Croat Policy of Persecution"? It was entirely your idea, your initiative to put that heading there and to set out what you set out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With no contribution at all from the lawyers?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that I can be clear on the matter, you haven't been, do correct me if I am wrong, you haven't been speaking with any other witnesses who might have been preparing their witness statements for the Defence, have you?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No, I am fairly independent in everything I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there's been no other lay, that is, non-lawyer coordinator of Defence witnesses as there may have been in other cases, but there's been no such coordinator of Defence witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: What period are you referring to? We met, Your Honours, before Christmas, myself and the Defence. I don't know the date that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. Have you, as a matter of interest, followed the trial of your former colleague and companion Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Only from the press when I had the time to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's received quite a lot of publicity, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness seems to be indicating. What is the problem? What is the problem, Mr. Robovic?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Not a problem. A the technical matter. I don't have the transcript. We are very busy with our own work so it's -- we follow the trial in a very sporadic way, at least I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you, nevertheless, have some idea of the issues at stake in this trial, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of the war, as you will be able to confirm, there were some people who made a considerable profit, financial profit out of that war, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: These are rumours. There are no accurate data, and this has been the case on all three sides, at least this is what people say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Take one notorious example. The name Fikret Abdic might be associated by many with profiteering in the war. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know Fikret Abdic personally well enough in order to be able to accept that. I have no comment on this at all, because I just don't know the person well enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're saying you don't know him well enough, but you do know him?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: We had coffee together, that is not in dispute. But I contend that I do not know him well enough. If it is enough to have had several coffee meetings with him, that is not enough to get to know a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Several coffee meetings. Can you tell us, please, what role Abdic had in relation to your party?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At any time?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: From what I know, he had -- he played no role. I am not even aware that he did anything in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall return to that, but help me with this. Where was your party based, geographically? Where was it founded and registered?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: In Mostar, in the higher court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it registered as based in Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No. In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't have any documents with you today, I imagine, showing one way or another where it was registered?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: All registration documents are with the higher court in Mostar. I believe it is still being kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because Kladusa, in the north-west of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is the hometown of Fikret Abdic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that from the press. I was never in Kladusa myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to press you again on Abdic's connection to your party. Your party remained in existence, as you tell us, until the Washington agreements; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's your party, and you were an active member of it, and you've given evidence about it. Am I right or wrong in suggesting to you that your party stayed into existence until -- stayed in active existence until it froze its activities, as you've described it, until the Washington agreements?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify it. We said in a meeting that when it concerns the Herceg-Bosna region, where I was the coordinator and where I was active, that is where the party will freeze its activities, and that was Armin Pohara's party. He was the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So at the very least, the party was active until the Washington agreement, and is this right: Some part of it may have been active thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, until the Washington Accords, and I'm not familiar with any activities of the party following the Washington Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One minute, please. Let's just deal with some of the personalities in your party. Pohara was the leader, wasn't he, in some way?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the party. I don't know about the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then was there a committee or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: There was a presidency. I think that that is what it was called. I cannot recall all the statutes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you were on the presidency, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can I give you some more names of people who may have been on that presidency, just to see if I've got it correct. Muhamed Alic, was he president of the Mostar party? Yes?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sulejman Salcinovic, from Derventa, party secretary?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know until what period. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then in addition to you, as members of the presidency, if such it was, Zlatko Udovicic; Edin, known as Edo, Omeragic; Muhidin Seric; Muhamed Kovacic; and Senad Dzonko? Yes?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they were in the presidency, but I believe that Zlatko Udovicic was, and Edo Omeragic also.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then, of course, the man Ismet Hadziosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many members did the party have?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know. I don't have the information. We tried to organise, but the crisis between the Muslims and Croats was coming to an end, and so these activities were then slowed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give us an idea. Is it a party of people in their tens, or people in their fifties, or even, I suppose, in their hundreds? Just how many members, very roughly, did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: A few. We did not have many members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was an extremely small group of people, was it not, so that you would know pretty well every member?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: More or less. There were a few people, but I'm not sure whether I could -- that I knew every single one. That I cannot accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so far as the members of whom you were aware, they were all, were they, driven by the same admirable motives that were driving you? Was that your judgement of them?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I only spoke about my own motives. I have my own motives, and this is what I talked about. I don't know about their own motives. But they had good intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And you don't have a bad word to say -- and I'm not complaining in this; I just want to check -- you don't have a bad word to say about any of the members of your party, small though it was, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything bad about some of the people you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we turn to one of the other members, a man by the name of Sead Pasic, you have nothing bad to say about him either, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: He was distributing humanitarian aid. This is what I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you know nothing to his discredit?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of interest and detail, is the man Zlatko Udovicic a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim. I don't know what he was born as, but he's a Muslim. His mother and his father were both Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When your party was formed, and thereafter, you had several contacts, did you not, in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with a party of a similar name, Croatian Muslim Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But your visits to Zagreb didn't stop dealing with the Muslim party, did they? You went and saw other people in Zagreb along with your president, Pohara.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people, there were some people from entertainment, there were some athletes, there were people who were beginning to be engaged in certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I'm concerned with your meetings with politicians. You went to the very top of the political life in Zagreb, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: At what level are you referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How about President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you really not understand me to be asking you all about meetings with political people when I was asking you about your meetings in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: It was one of them. There was many of them, but as far as the politics was concerned, yes, but I have had meetings of a different kind. Politics is only one type of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know from following this trial, Mr. Robovic, that included in the issues at stake is the degree to which Tudjman was running affairs in Central Bosnia. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your reading of the press reports of this case and your contact with the lawyers has never revealed that to you?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many visits did you, with your very small party of Muslims, make to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I was there twice, that I am certain of. There may have been a third meeting but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Pohara, your president, may well have been there more often.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: He was there with me twice, but I don't know of others, he never revealed that to me. He may have been there with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it not occur to you in this summary that you tell us you drafted yourself to mention the fact that at the establishment of your party, you had been meeting the president of the neighbouring state of Croatia? Did it not occur to you to mention that?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever occurred to me, I put down in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, as a matter of fact -- I don't want to know any more than this -- discuss with the lawyers for Kordic the fact that you'd seen Tudjman? That's yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, tell us, please, what was Tudjman's interest in your small party?

utterances.speaker: ZULFO ROBOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know what his interests consisted in, but we were looking for certain solutions, and we went knocking on every door in order to effect the cessation of hostilities between the Croats and Muslims and whoever was placed high, we would go to such person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he say, did Tudjman say, please?
