I have Mr. Guariglia with me, who has helped me drafting on the legal side of things, and if you want any assistance on that beyond what's contained in the brief, I'd ask him to have leave to address you. But no, overall there's just simply the question of relevance to these proceedings and these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it must be said that this is the report, the reports, about a witness, the reports 15 years before he gave evidence, and 16 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I suppose it would be open to you to say that you should be able to call expert evidence on whether this illness is likely to persist over a period of 15 to 16 years. It may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I had an expert as opposed to a record producer, and if there was one properly before the Court, I could probably ask him that and save one tending. But, yes, I might. Although I'd be anxious not to use time and money doing that, yes, I suppose I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think, as I said yesterday, Mr. President, we are producing Dr. Pavlovic to authenticate medical records from a work institute. These are public records. We're not producing him to render an expert opinion. I believe that he sat on the board which considered Mr. Cicak's eligibility to work. It's significant that the eligibility for fitness to work was a determination made, I believe, in 1984, which is actually only a few years before the events about which Mr. Cicak testified in this court, 1991, 1992 being the operative time periods. So first of all, he's produced to lay the foundation for those documents and to authenticate them, upon objection of the Prosecution. Second, he's not produced to offer expert testimony. Third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pausing there, he does, as I say, comment upon the illness. He mentions -- certainly his affidavit mentions his -- the effect of the illness and it's manifestations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think he mentions its manifestations, most definitely. But I would have thought, Your Honour, that is a matter of absolutely no controversy. Those are medical facts. This is a medical witness. I cannot imagine that the manifestations of the syndrome are actually contested. But if they are, then we can bring an expert witness doctor along who can testify about what those manifestations are, if it's necessary. I would just add two final points, Your Honour. There was a considerable amount of -- well, I won't -- let me put it neutrally too, non-responsiveness with respect to the questions asked of this witness by the bench as to whether he retired and, if so, why. And he was very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is true, and he claimed not to be able to remember at what age he retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Or why, Your Honour. And actually, the second point that I wanted to make was related to the privacy concern and it's also related to this point. It has been a witness from Busovaca, a Mr. Maric, who testified about being acquainted with this particular witness, and actually having the witness tell him that he had retired as a result of a psychiatric disability. And he proceeded to explain to Mr. Maric, and actually show him documents that we believe were generated by the very institute that we're talking about, which chronicled his complaints, and Mr. Cicak described the effects of this malady upon him, being unable to contain his temper and so forth. So any privacy concerns, I think, have to be considered against that backdrop. The very individual who would be asserting those concerns apparently has no hesitation in describing the syndrome and showing documents related to that syndrome to others.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. So any privacy concerns, I think, have been waived by the witness himself to the extent that there are any privacy concerns.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just transfer to the French channel, if I may. And also these determinations were made by a work board. These are not his individual physicians. The considerations of the doctor/patient privilege I suppose coming from the jurisdiction that I come from, do not apply in this particular category because it was a vocational or a vocational fitness that was being considered by a dually appointed panel of physicians. And I believe, as I've said in my previous submission, that this was a determination that was subject to appeal, so these are actually public records; they're not private records. So for all of those reasons, we are prepared to bring Dr. Pavlovic. As I say, my direct examination of the doctor will last about two minutes, and as to the cross-examination, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's another point which I haven't raised, which is the point about collateral issues. Certainly, there is a rule in the United Kingdom, I don't know about the United States, which prevents calling a lot of evidence about side issues, collateral issues. If we go down the road of calling evidence about witnesses' credibility, is there not the danger that the Trial Chamber, or any court, is likely to be distracted and time taken up about the pursuit of what may not be terribly important issues and are essentially secondary? After all, his evidence was in a very limited area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, of course, Your Honour, the point that you make has considerable -- in fact, it has very considerable force. And there is a rule in the United States as there is in England, I'm sure, regarding collateral issues. If this issue had not been raised during the course of the witness' examination we might not find ourselves in the position of having to offer this evidence but the issue was raised. In fact, it was raised by us in cross-examination. The witness refused to answer the question. The bench pressed him on the point, and he tried to wiggle out of it with an answer that was, we think, just completely incorrect. And therefore we think that that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we needn't trouble you any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm hoping to address you on some of the subjects to be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because if you are minded to allow this witness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The points that have been raised, in our respectful submission, don't go anywhere near meeting the realities of this case. First of all, yes, he was reluctant or plainly worse about the date of his retirement. That may be because he was embarrassed, who knows. But that being said, there is no relevance in the issue of his mental state. It wasn't raised with him. Kordic engaged in polemic -- in the newspapers with him, and treated him as a person with whom to engage in debate without ever accusing him of being intellectually or mentally unwell. The Chamber will also recall that there was a curious passage in the cross-examination where the Chamber was concerned about whether it was being accepted that Cicak had been beaten up or not. And it was eventually drawn from the Defence that no there wasn't any challenge that to the fact that he was beaten up, he was beaten up. And the only issue was what, if anything, had been said beforehand by Kordic to acknowledge his responsibility tacitly or otherwise to what had gone on. So mental issues simply didn't arise, stale as they were. So the relevance issue is really top of this particular agenda. Obviously, if any issues of Cicak's behaviour at the time being linked with mental condition were going to be raised, they should have been put expressly and they simply weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The relevance is as to credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But they simply weren't put to him at all. And he really should have a chance to deal with those because Your Honour says well, we might seek to deal with it through an expert. We might also seek to deal with it through him. The point on privacy isn't met at all. The fact that somebody may show documents to a private individual, if that individual is right in the evidence that is gained, says nothing about the entitlement of a court to look at those documents without the consent of the person concerned. We haven't approached Cicak about this yet, but it certainly shouldn't be done without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, it doesn't seem to be very much different from what one obtains certainly in Jamaica and, I believe, in the United Kingdom where a civil servant goes before a medical board and can be retired by the medical board on grounds of ill health, and I think Mr. Sayers is right, that in such circumstances, that's not private.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the documents that underlie that relate to medical examination are. Neither you nor I would expect nor find documents on us dealing with our medical conditions produced for the purposes of employment, say, here suddenly produced in the course of litigation elsewhere if it is apprised. I must say, were that to happen, and I would take personally every step I could, if I so judged it appropriate, to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not so sure you are right, because that is done -- well, in Jamaica by virtue of a law which provides for it, and I don't think it is -- it's private anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we must disagree on that or we may disagree on that. But the problems of allowing this evidence in, particularly if you allow it in as to the last paragraph of what is there on paragraph 14 of this affidavit which is, I think, the passage Your Honour Judge May was referring to when you said it was effectively commenting on his performance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I was dealing at the time with paragraph 14 and the Court sees the problem there, because if that's going to be raised in any sense by a side wind or otherwise, I'm entitled to and probably will explore matters in whatever detail I think is appropriate, taken whatever time is appropriate, calling rebuttal expert evidence if it is appropriate. Now, the mere bare fact -- I'm so sorry. The mere bare fact of his retirement on medical grounds might, itself, be unexceptional and no doubt if it had been put to him in terms, "You were retired on medical grounds on this date," he probably would have then said yes and that would be the end of it. Can this evidence go any further? Answer: No. This is a clear effort to undermine Cicak's evidence by stale psychiatric evidence which is going to be a form of an opinion evidence on this man's testimony however it's dressed up. That can't help you. You saw the man. This is an issue for the Trial Chamber and it cannot be assisted by being told that the man was retired for these reasons however many years before. Even before we reach the procedural and legal difficulties that are thrown up including, and I'll just identify them for you for your consideration, those that we set out in paragraph six when turning to the European laws approached in these issues. So our very respectful submission is that this evidence shouldn't be allowed and it may well -- I have no idea what I'll do if it's allowed in, and I'm not -- it's never been my disposition to try and hold the Court in any way at ransom. I don't know what I will do, but I do know that I will raise it with Mr. Cicak if this matter goes before the Court and he may have something he wants to say to that, not the least may be his concern how they ever got a hold of these documents. That would certainly be my concern. And overall, the evidence simply can't help. For what, may I just repeat, for what reason is this being laid before unless it's to found an argument, in due course, this man may, so many years later, have been paranoid. Simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, normally the rule which we have -- which I have mentioned about collateral issues applies, but in this particular case, certainly the cross-examination and the examination took an unusual course in that the witness refused, really, to answer questions on the topic claiming he didn't know, claiming at one stage that he'd never been to a doctor. So the issue was raised, and we've come to the conclusion that as a matter of fairness, his evidence should be called. But having regard to the privacy issues which have been raised, we have in mind that it should be done in closed session since we've got the ability to do that here, and that the exhibits should remain under seal. That will ensure that these matters are not made public. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. On that topic, I'll tell Mr. Cicak that. I'm not sure that I will be in a position, finally, to deal with the witness when he's now listed for next week. I shall make all efforts to do so, but I don't rule out the possibility that there will be other applications maybe by Mr. Cicak himself, I can't promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They certainly won't be encouraged because we've considered all the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the next issue is the question of the state of the affidavits. What I have in mind is that we've had -- we had three affidavits filed in the week of June the 5th, Mr. Pelivan and Mr. Jukic and Mr. -- I'll have to be reminded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, Mr. Goludza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Goludza, that's the name, thank you. Thank you. And since then we've had two further affidavits which we need not trouble about at the moment although, Mr. Sayers, I draw to your attention that both are numbered 29, and that can't be right, but that's a small point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We started our preparation for the first three witnesses, but as they are also in support of this week's witnesses, we aren't in a position to complete our dealings with them and, indeed, we should have -- technically we should have whatever seven days from the witnesses in support of whom they are tendered and so we can't do our analysis of their utility yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Next week then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next week, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And perhaps you can deal with all the witnesses, all the affidavits. The last two are -- yes, Mr. Nusbaurm is in support of these two witnesses who have just given evidence and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is support of the next witness, so we'll deal with them all next week. And that brings us to the final point which is Mr. Kovacic, you -- we started yesterday on the issue of when it will be convenient to start your case and we have in mind the 24th of July since the other case will finish during the week previously. Now, if you want to address us on that, of course, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to say a few words. I believe we already talked about it some three weeks ago and it was the first time that it was mentioned that Kordic's Defence might move on faster -- quicker than planned, and then we were asked if Mr. Cerkez's Defence could take up as soon as they were finished. I'm sorry to say that I was overly optimistic on that occasion, because that's the kind of man that I am. And then I said that I thought that we could do that. I still stand by that what I said on that occasion, but I should like to ask you to bear in mind the following. According to the instructions received from the Chamber, we were told what the calendar would be and we planned from the day onward to proceed with the case immediately after the summer recess. When this second option arose recently, we did try to go into it but, unfortunately, we ran into some problems and I must tell you about it. First of all, our organisation, some people that we counted upon will not be available at that time so we shall have to reshape our team and that is all that easy. And secondly, which only makes it worse, last week I went to Vitez, and I'll explained why it was only as late as last week. That is of five witnesses, three told me they could not come in July because earlier I had told them that they'd had to come in September, so they already had plans of their own. Of course, we could bring in some other witnesses, perhaps change our schedule slightly and call some other people. However, I should like to take this opportunity that we shall do our utmost to start then on that occasion because it's not two weeks earlier, it's six weeks earlier, so it does affect our preparations seriously, but we shall indeed do our utmost to try to be ready for that new date. However, I need to say that it will be somewhat at our expense because simply that we shall not be able to present our case in a logical manner by following some logical entities or to move from one subject to the other. We shall have to be jumping from one to another, but perhaps it will not cause too much trouble to you because you have already heard too many stories about 1992 and then 1992-1993. We shall not be the first ones to begin with that, but I'm not very happy with this. I'm not very happy not because I am optimistically minded, but simply because I do not think that we shall be able to present our case in the best possible manner. Secondly, after we discussed it first, we already undertook some steps to organise our work better, but you must have heard that Zagreb, and I suppose you have heard it from other sources not only from me, that in Zagreb, documents are distributed widely. But the problem is that they are issued in a very strange way. That one day we have one procedure applied, there is one protocol. So that two men of mine, and I am talking in terms of man hours, and they spent 16 man hours going through some old, smelly, moldy documents having heard some promises from the state, and then what it comes down to is that those -- that they could have spent that fortnight somewhere at the seaside and had a good rest. Because we have not been issued with these documents because meanwhile the state has changed the "owner" of these documents, so the fact that we've made a list of documents we needed they tell us, "Forget it," because these are documents from a different state agency, so you have to apply there and through all those documents again. So we have suffered a tremendous injustice because we were promised that any documents that was being shown to the Prosecution, because they are being the same thing in the other room, that we would be given a copy of that. And the other way around, that the Prosecution would be getting the copies of all documents that we go through. Now, of course, I am not accusing anybody. I'm not saying that the Prosecution has received documents that we had marked and were denied them but, unfortunately, I have to say that I have not been given any paper of 8.000, and that is roughly the number that was given by the person charged by the new Croatian state with publishing those documents, 8.000 have been published. I do not have a single copy of those. We, of course, have limited resources, but the thing is I had two men sitting there for 16 hours a day with no result whatsoever. They could have worked in Vitez instead. We could have changed our schedule, our calendar, our witnesses, and all that, and instead of having quite a few documents that are available in Vitez, we wasted all this time. And these are terrible problems because we are preparing our case, our Defence. We already had the concept of the Defence as of the first day, and now there are some documents we've only seen, but not yet been -- which have not been released to us which will mean additional work, additional effort, additional witnesses who may be figuring in some of those documents. I'm saying this simply because I have to ask you for some flexibility in compiling my -- in finalising my list of witnesses because some new issues are coming up. Not only those that arose during the Prosecution's case, but now some new questions which seem to be cropping up with those new documents. And my lawyer's nose, my experience tells me that the Prosecution is now using some information derived from those documents for shortly, perhaps not having to do with my client, but that may be something that has to do with my client, yet we do not have these documents at all. So we are dealing with a new theory of disclosure which I have not seen yet. I do not know about it. I'm not sure about it. But there are some indications that there is something like that now which is playing now. We did exchange some correspondence with the Prosecution and we did clarify the matter of one document, but that document came from another office that is specifically from the president's office. And I really, to be quite candid, have no idea what goes on there, and the information I receive is that they are disclosing documents by boxes. I don't know what happens there, but I think I have to see those documents, because I do not know whether these boxes contain the death sentence for my client or the acquittal sentence. My men are running from one door to the other. They're getting all sorts of promises and faxes and whatnots, but I still do not have any concrete promise. Nothing has happened. I'm not asking for anything else but some tolerance, but some forebearance, and especially we are asking for additional freedom in making the list of our witnesses. And another matter which I wish to raise, although I believe I've raised it already before: I think that the Prosecution has introduced documents Z2813.2 and Z2332.1. Those were the so-called Spork binders, if I may remind you. They included a number of lists. One of such lists was a list of some 4.500 individuals, I believe. And it is implied, basically, that every individual on that list was a member of the Vitez Brigade. And to present a caricature, the Prosecutor is now trying to persuade me that person A on that list, and we have some testimony that he did something elicit, was a soldier subordinate to the accused Cerkez. I tried to challenge the list as much as I could at that time, explicitly. For technical reasons, we simply could not get all those 4.500 names. Now we're faced with an absurd situation. Theoretically, I should bring here about 2.500 witness, or affidavits -- it doesn't matter -- who would say: At that time shown in the list I was there and I was a member of such-and-such unit and we were there. We also had some witnesses -- I do not know which ones testified under protective measures. No. We had two witnesses, Buha and Santic, for instance, one of these days, who were members of Vitezovi, and they said in so many words -- they said that in so many words here before this Court. They are on that list. We also had a witness who was a member of the Operative Zone -- command of the Operative Zone, Nakic, Franjo Nakic, if you recall. He's also on the list. So now, rather than by majorities, proving one by one, I don't think it is possible. So what we have to do is show that it is probable that the list is not what it is presumed to be. So I have to present 40 or 50 affidavits of witnesses who will say: It was shown that I was on the list such-and-such, but at that time I wasn't there; I was in a different place. To bring two or three lay witnesses and then try to explain the reasons for which this list came up, which are the motives underlying that list. And then the key issue, but that is the conventional evidence, and I don't want to tire you with it. That is that the list does not show it clearly that this 22nd Domobran Regiment was the legal successor to the Vitez Brigade. In point of fact, that list is a legal successor to all sorts of not only military units, but also non-military units, that is, all sorts of groups of population who for some reason or other had some rights or thought they had some rights. But I'm using it only by way of an example, to show that it is very difficult to really define certain matters. And I really would be ashamed of trying to bring here 2.500 affidavits, even if technically I was up to it. And I do not think it is, in a matter of three months or something like that. But that will be a major problem. It will be a major hindrance in my case. Of course, I have to face up to it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Kovacic. I'm not quite -- what is important, it's not you are telling us about incredible figures, 2.500, 4.500, and so on and so forth, but it suffices, I think, one should -- all that has to be proven is the association between your client and your list. And there are other conditions. But the fact that somebody is on the list, it will establish or not establish association with the accused. You cannot take this list as one of the -- as the charge against your client. I think everything has to be put in its proper place. You know law, so you know there are certain criteria to associate a person with something, even if this is a superior person to somebody else who has committed whatever crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours, and I'm glad to hear it from you. But being a cautious lawyer myself, I have to try to put down my defence on the first front line. If that one falls, then I have to go back to the second one. But that is one of the criteria, and that is -- I mean, that is what the list looks like, prima facie. There are some persons who are "recognised," in inverted commas, as members of my brigade. But I'm not talking about it, basically. What I'm saying is that this kind of exhibit, which to my mind lacks seriousness, but nevertheless it forces me to some investigation. And I never dreamed that I would have to go to investigate that at the time when the Prosecution was still some five weeks away before the conclusion of their case. And unfortunately, that is the reality. And if one adds to it these documents in Zagreb that I've just mentioned, that is unfortunately the reality, which makes me very unhappy. I hope we shall be able to somehow come to grips with it by investing more effort into it, and we shall do that. But bearing in mind all that, I should like to ask you to grant me some more flexibility. But simply objectively speaking, we shall not be able to really determine which witnesses we need, which we do not need. I shall not be able to put -- to finalise my list of witnesses. I'm simply unable to do it, because our theory about a fixed list of witnesses -- and I know you showed major tolerance, but that theory is based on that whole theory of regular and timely disclosure, and we are still lacking it, because the disclosure is still at issue here. I'm not attacking now the Prosecutor's office. Both they and we are now faced with this avalanche of new documents which are being disclosed. So that is my problem. I hope I was clear enough. But perhaps I should add just one thing more, simply for the sake of better planning. If you decide so, we shall of course begin on that date. But in view of some organisation -- I'm really quite candid. I'm not trying to use any tactics now -- even if we began in September, after the recess, I do not think it would be the loss of two weeks of work, because I'm talking about a fortnight of work. It could have been perhaps a loss of one week's work, which would enable us to better organise things. But that is just by the way. Thank you. Of course, I'm quite ready to answer any questions that you might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I be heard one on point? I've got three points I want to make, but on this one point, there's one thing I wanted to say yesterday, as I think of considerable importance, and it leads to my asking the Chamber not to allow any downtime, as it were, before the summer recess, for this reason: The documents that are being produced to all parties in Zagreb are likely -- I can't say very likely, but are likely to involve not only some evidence in rebuttal, because there's already other evidence in rebuttal, but quite possibly a very considerable quantity of evidence in rebuttal of necessity. I've said right from the beginning of this case that if Croatia ever honoured its obligations and produced documents, that that might be the best material available to the Chamber, and it therefore simply will cry out for, if not demand, consideration. And documents may or may not come in on their own. They may inevitably lead to further live witnesses. So the rebuttal case may well be substantial. Now, the time that -- the timetable we're on already, going to the end of October and then two weeks off, is extremely tight to finish by Christmas. Obviously everyone will want to finish by Christmas, and there may be very particular problems if we go beyond Christmas in this case, being staffed by the same personnel and so on. But if we lose two weeks before the summer recess, I think the chances of finishing this case by Christmas become increasingly limited, and I'm very concerned about that. It is hard work for all of us to go straight from one case to the next, in the same way as it's very hard, frankly, to be keeping up with this flow of evidence at the moment, but we're all doing it in order that we can finish this case expeditiously. And I would urge the Chamber -- it happens to be not what I would like personally, but I would urge the Chamber, for practical reasons, not to allow any gap between one case and the next. That would, of course, involve a Pre-Trial hearing at some stage to be slipped in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You said you had some other points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other points are entirely separate. Shall I mention them now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with this. Mr. Kovacic, we hear what you say, and of course we bear in mind the problems that you mention, particularly the fact that there may be -- there is further disclosure, which will make things difficult. But we also have in mind the necessity of finishing this case and the view of the International Community, which is watching this institution. And if another two weeks disappear, there is bound to be justified criticism. Not that that, of course, has an effect on the fairness of the trial, which is the matter which we have to determine, but these are matters all of which we have to have in mind. We shall require you to start on the 24th, doing the best you can. If there are further difficulties, we'll hear about them from you and of course we'll consider the position, and there may be a degree of flexibility. But we would wish to occupy, if at all possible, those two weeks, and I'm sure you will do what you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kovacic. Microphone for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But that was exactly my point. I can do it. Yes, I need a lot of additional resources, organisation, additional talks to the witnesses. But the point is, I will need for that a certain flexibility, because, as you are, I was also very exact of the arguments you mention. There is no sense to make this sense [sic] longer, and certainly I don't want to be a cause for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have three other short points. One actually goes back to the witness we were discussing, the medical witness we were discussing. A few weeks ago, when I first raised it, I raised, with some concern, the fact that the affidavit, with associated documents, had been filed publicly, meaning that the document will be available, as such documents are to any member of the public, to view. The Court has now made an order, or forecast making an order, that the evidence of the witness will be given in closed session in order that that material should be protected. We've spoken this afternoon in open session, and every step should now be taken to protect, from this moment onwards, the material concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That will be done. That's already in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the other two points are these. We've now got a list of the witnesses from the Kordic Defence up until the week of July 3rd. I repeat my request yesterday. As somebody who served, quite voluntarily, six weeks and then months of witnesses, that really we should have, and it will help the preparation of this case if we can have the final batting list of all witnesses up till the end of the case plainly known by the Defence, and there's no reason for us not to have it. And the final request is this: The experts' reports have been provided to us in English. We've asked for them in B/C/S, both because we want to be sure, whether they exist in B/C/S, that there are proper translations, and it seems inevitable that they must exist in B/C/S for the defendant himself to read them. We also may need them -- or may prefer them to be in B/C/S because if we are putting them to experts who are themselves linguists in that language -- users of that language -- we're told that no such reports exist in B/C/S, but we would be grateful for them if they do exist, as it will help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Responding to the last point first, Your Honour. We don't have the expert reports in Croatian. They can always be submitted, I suppose, to the Translation Unit if it's absolutely necessary, but I can't imagine that it is. If I might just respond to the forecast that there appears to be a move under foot to put on another case in chief by representations that we're going to have a substantial rebuttal case. I've prepared a little chart and I'll have it for the Court tomorrow. The longest rebuttal that's been permitted in any of the Lasva Valley cases to date I believe is four days, and it consisted of two witnesses, and I think that was in the Blaskic case. I would certainly hope that we're not going to be looking at this case as the -- I think I've said it earlier in a pleading -- the criminal equivalent of a case of Jarndyce versus Jarndyce, a case that never ends. This case has got to come to an end at some point, and I would certainly hope that after an indictment was prepared, I believe, in 1995, presumably on the basis that the Prosecution had enough evidence to convict at that point, there is simply no excuse for prolonging these proceedings any further than they absolutely need to be. And so I would certainly hope that the Court would bear in mind, when it considers the length of the rebuttal case, the kinds of rebuttal cases that have been put on these cases to date, and two other things: the length of time that the indictment has been outstanding, and also, and much more important from the perspective of my client, the amount of time that he's been in gaol already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll sit again at half past 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
